result.markdown: --- title: "Sensitivity and identifiability" course-unit: ch11-sensitivity-and-identifiability status: complete --- ## Why this unit matters - **Sensitivity:** which inputs move a chosen output? - **Identifiability:** which parameters can the observation process distinguish? - A narrow optimizer interval is not evidence that every biological parameter is learned. ::: {.notes} Three minutes, and set the shape of the session: three tools, one question each. Local sensitivity asks what happens if I nudge a parameter. Global sensitivity asks which parameter is responsible for the spread in outcomes across a whole plausible range. Structural identifiability asks a different kind of question altogether: not what the model does, but what the data could ever tell us about it. Keep one distinction visible all session, because everything here turns on it: perturbing a model is not the same as learning from data. This is also the last slot of a long day, so promise the payoff early. The session ends by proving something about this afternoon's reporting fraction. ::: ## Baseline SIR model Deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population model: $$ \dot S=-\beta cSI/N,\qquad \dot I=\beta cSI/N-\gamma I,\qquad \dot R=\gamma I. $$ At the course baseline, $N=1000$, $(S,I,R)=(990,10,0)$, $(\beta,c,\gamma)=(0.05,10,0.25)$, and $\mathcal R_0=\beta c/\gamma=2$. The state sensitivity matrix is $J_x(t)=\partial x(t)/\partial(\beta,c,\gamma)$. ::: {.notes} Two minutes. Same baseline as every other session, so nothing here is new except the notation for the sensitivity matrix. Plant one seed and move on: beta and c never appear apart in these equations, only as the product beta-c. Ask the room what that might mean for estimating them separately, take one answer, and say the last part of the session settles it. One warning about the parameterisation: from here the code uses a positional vector [beta, c, gamma] rather than the named tuple of the earlier sessions, because the sensitivity and Sobol APIs index parameters by position. The worksheet flags this too. ::: ## Local sensitivity: a derivative, not an uncertainty interval For a small perturbation, $$ \Delta z\approx\nabla_\theta z\,\Delta\theta. $$ Raw derivatives carry the units of their own parameter: since the model uses only $k=\beta c$, $\partial I/\partial\beta=c\,\partial I/\partial k$ and $\partial I/\partial c=\beta\,\partial I/\partial k$, a factor $c/\beta=200$ apart wherever they are nonzero. The elasticity $(\theta_j/I)\,\partial I/\partial\theta_j$ is dimensionless and comparable across parameters. ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch10-local .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch10-local .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Centered local derivatives of infectious prevalence, raw and as dimensionless elasticities. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Eight minutes, and the curves are worth reading aloud rather than summarising. Each one is the derivative of infectious prevalence with respect to one parameter, over time. They start at zero, since at day zero nothing has happened yet, peak around the epidemic peak, and change sign afterwards, because raising transmission moves the epidemic *earlier* as well as higher, so late in the window a bigger beta means fewer people still infectious. Read the left panel first and let the room fall into the trap. Beta looks overwhelming and c looks like a flat line at zero. Ask whether that means beta matters more, then spring it: the two curves differ by exactly two hundred, which is c over beta. Beta is measured per contact and c in contacts per day, so the derivatives are in different units and the comparison is meaningless. Nudging beta by 0.01 is a twenty percent change; nudging c by 0.01 is nothing at all. The right panel divides that out, asking instead for the percentage change in I per percentage change in each parameter. Now beta and c lie exactly on top of each other, which is why c is dashed — otherwise it would be invisible. That coincidence is the session in one picture: nothing in this plot could tell the two apart, and Worksheet Part A has them verify it numerically. Two warnings. This is a derivative at one parameter vector, so it says nothing about behaviour a long way from the baseline; that is the next slide. And a derivative is not an uncertainty interval and not a posterior; a large derivative means a parameter matters, not that we know it badly. ::: ## Global variation: sharing out the variance Vary all three parameters across a plausible box and ask how much of the *variance* in peak prevalence each one accounts for: - $S_1$: the share that parameter explains **on its own**. - $S_T$: its share **including every interaction** it takes part in. $S_T > S_1$ means the parameter matters in combination with others; $\sum_i S_1^i < 1$ is the part of the variance no single parameter owns. ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch10-global .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch10-global .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` One-at-a-time swings and Sobol indices over the same parameter box. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Ten minutes, and it is the heart of the session. Walk the left panel first: move one parameter from the bottom of its range to the top, holding the others at baseline, and record the swing. It gives a ranking, and it is what most people do by hand. Then say what it cannot see: it never leaves the baseline for the other two parameters, so a parameter that only matters when transmission is already high looks unimportant. The right panel varies all three together. Point at the gap between the blue and orange bars: that gap is interaction. Here the first-order shares sum to roughly 0.85 — nearer 0.89 on a far larger design — so of the order of a tenth of the variance belongs to no parameter individually. Both panels depend entirely on the box; widen the bounds and the ranking can change, which is the caveat to state out loud. One caveat that the next slide will sharpen. Beta and c get separate bars here only because we sampled them as two independent uniforms, and the sizes of those bars follow from the two boxes we chose, not from anything the model distinguishes. Sobol answers which input ranges drive the spread in the output; it never answers which parameters could be estimated. Anyone reading a taller beta bar as "we can measure beta" has confused the two questions, which is exactly what the observation map settles next. Two footnotes if asked. The package warns that its design matrices are not fully independent QMC sequences; that is suppressed here for legibility and does not change the picture at this sample size. And 500 samples is deliberate: the worksheet repeats this at 32 and shows the indices are unstable, even negative, when the sample is too small. ::: ## The observation map Only incidence is observed: $$ y(t)=\beta c\,S(t)I(t)/N. $$ The transformation $(\beta,c)\mapsto(a\beta,c/a)$ leaves this map unchanged. Thus $\beta$ and $c$ are structurally confounded; $\beta c$ can be learned. The reporting fraction $\rho$ from the previous session is the same argument with a twist: observing $\rho C(t)$, the pair $(\rho,\beta c)$ is confounded **only if the initial state is unknown**. Treat $S(0), I(0), R(0), C(0)$ as known and both become identifiable. Background knowledge, not more data, is what buys it. ::: {.notes} Eight minutes. This is the payoff for the observation-models session, so name the callback explicitly: this afternoon we said a small epidemic fully reported and a large one partly reported look alike, and here is the precise version. Be accurate about the twist, because it is the interesting part. Scaling the whole population up and the reporting fraction down leaves the observed counts unchanged, so with unknown initial conditions only the ratio survives. Declaring the initial state breaks that symmetry, and the worksheet runs both cases and gets exactly that. Say "the initial state", not "the population size": the worksheet marks all four initial values known, which is a stronger assumption than knowing $N$ alone. The lesson is that identifiability is a property of the model *plus* what you already know, not of the equations alone. Contrast with the beta-c case above, which no amount of external knowledge about population size repairs. There you need contact data or an independently measured c. ::: ## API and validation The derivatives above came from finite differences. The library computes them directly, by solving the variational equations alongside the model: ::: {#cell-ch10-forward-sensitivity .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#ch10-forward-sensitivity .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (saved_times = 41, relative_difference = 7.0e-5) ``` ::: ::: - `SciMLSensitivity`: forward sensitivities or adjoints. - `GlobalSensitivity`: Sobol first-order and total indices. - `StructuralIdentifiability`: `assess_identifiability`, run in the worksheet. - Validate: check $S+I+R=N$, and one derivative two ways, as above. ::: {.notes} Five minutes. The point of running this live is that the augmented problem and the finite differences agree to about one part in ten thousand, so the earlier plot was not an artefact of the perturbation size, and you now have the API that scales to models where finite differences would be hopeless. Worth one aside if the room is with you: that agreement needs tight solver tolerances on both slides. A centered difference subtracts two trajectories that differ in the fifth decimal place, so at the default tolerances the same comparison only agrees to a couple of percent, and the error is in the finite difference, not in the library. That is the practical argument for the variational equations even when a finite difference is available. The one API not executed here is `assess_identifiability`: it compiles for tens of seconds on a cold session, which is not something to do in front of an audience. That is why it lives in the worksheet, and why the warm-up cell during the break matters. Say that out loud rather than skipping past it. ::: ## Takeaways and limitations - Local: neighborhood behavior around one parameter vector. - Global: ranking conditional on ranges and a design. - Structural: information available in an idealized observation map, and in what you already know, such as the initial state. - Practical identifiability also depends on noise, sampling, initial states, and misspecification. Read the [book chapter](../../chapters/11-sensitivity-and-identifiability.html) for derivations and exercises; see the [SciMLSensitivity](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLSensitivity/stable/), [GlobalSensitivity](https://docs.sciml.ai/GlobalSensitivity/stable/), and [StructuralIdentifiability](https://docs.sciml.ai/StructuralIdentifiability/stable/) documentation for APIs. ::: {.notes} Four minutes, and it is the last thing anyone hears on Day 2, so land it rather than reading the bullets. Ask which of the session's conclusions are about the model and which are about the data. The Sobol ranking is about the model and the box we chose; the identifiability results are about the data and what we already know. Confusing the two is how people end up reporting a confident estimate of a quantity their data never contained. Then hand over to tomorrow: sensitivity tells you which parameter to spend effort on, and the intervention session asks what to do about it. Flag that Part C of the worksheet is where the reporting-fraction result gets proved, and that the two inference chapters it points at are self-study, not sessions here. :::
